questions.q: Why does this lesson treat the written report as the real deliverable, not paperwork added on top of the testing work?
options: Because clients never read technical sections regardless of how they're written
Because stakeholders who weren't in the room act on the document, and a poorly written finding gets argued with, deprioritized, or ignored
Because regulators require reports to be a fixed page count
Because the lab environment itself is destroyed after testing, so only the report survives
questions.explain: Decision-makers, engineers who fix the issue, and possibly auditors only ever see the report -- a sloppy write-up undermines even a brilliant finding.

questions.q: What belongs in the executive summary, according to this lesson?
options: The exact Nmap and Metasploit command syntax used during testing
The full CVSS vector string for every finding
Raw terminal output from the exploitation session
The business-risk framing -- what's wrong, how bad it is, and how fast it needs fixing -- without CVE IDs or tool names
questions.explain: The executive summary is written for a reader who will never open the technical section, so it stays in business-risk terms.

questions.q: In Finding 1's CVSS vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H, what does showing the vector string alongside the 9.8 score actually accomplish?
options: It specifies exactly which metrics (like no privileges required, low attack complexity) justify why the finding scored Critical instead of High
It encrypts the finding so only the client's CISO can read it
It is purely decorative and has no effect on how the finding is read
It replaces the need for a written description of the vulnerability
questions.explain: The vector string's individual metrics are the actual justification for the score; the number alone doesn't show the reasoning.

questions.q: Why does the remediation recommendations section order findings into a prioritized schedule rather than just listing them?
options: Findings must always appear in the order they were discovered during testing
Alphabetical ordering is required by every industry reporting standard
A prioritized schedule with realistic timeframes turns the report into an executable project plan instead of leaving the client guessing what to fix first
Ordering has no real effect on how a client acts on the report
questions.explain: Severity-based ordering with timeframes is what makes a report something a client can actually execute against, not just read.

questions.q: According to this lesson's pre-delivery checklist, what must be true before a penetration test report goes out?
options: Only the executive summary needs to be reviewed; technical findings can skip review
Every finding is independently reproducible from the evidence given, no live credentials or unredacted sensitive data appear anywhere, and the client's named technical contact has reviewed it
The report must omit CVSS scores entirely to avoid alarming the client
Live credentials discovered during testing should be included so the client can verify them
questions.explain: Reproducibility, redaction of sensitive data, and a technical-contact review pass are the non-negotiable checks before a report is considered final.
